entry.englishMeaning: to display pride or self-satisfaction, especially to impress others
entry.coreIdea: Show off how pleased you are with yourself.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Figurative verb for displaying self-satisfaction, drawing on the image of a bird grooming its feathers.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Usually negative in this human sense: it suggests vanity or excessive pride.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Self-questioning and critical here: the speaker rejects showing off as a worthwhile aim.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Expressive vocabulary in commentary and description. “Show off” is more common in casual speech.

when_to_use: Use preen critically or playfully when someone openly enjoys admiration and shows excessive pride.
It suits descriptions of a person reacting smugly to praise or success.
when_not_to_use: Do not use preen as neutral praise for someone's confidence; it often suggests vanity.
Quiet satisfaction after hard work need not be described as preening.

advanced_nuance: Preen can be humorous rather than harsh, but it still draws attention to self-admiration.
In the source, preen describes a rejected motive. The sentence does not establish that someone actually behaved this way.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture someone lingering in the spotlight, delighted by the applause.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: He preened in front of the audience instead of thanking his team.
memory_practice.recall_question: Why might calling someone preening sound critical?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Who is preening? A: Someone quietly thanks the team. B: Someone keeps drawing attention to their own brilliance. Explain the attitude suggested.
memory_practice.production_task: Describe a fictional character reacting to praise. Use preen and include one detail that shows visible self-satisfaction.

examples.example_1: He preened in front of the cameras after accepting the award.
examples.example_2: She preened herself on her clever answer while the rest of the team waited to speak.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: He has mentioned that award five times today.
B: Yes, he's still preening after yesterday's ceremony.
A: I hope we can get back to the project now.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: Oh  yeah,  I  guess  it's  not  to  make  the  other  person  squirm  or  to  preen  in  fr ont  of  a  crowd .
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to display pride or self-satisfaction, especially to impress others
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker rejects showing off in front of an audience as a reason for having the conversation.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Calling a modest person who simply accepts thanks someone who preens can sound unfairly critical.
mistakes_differences.correction: Use preen when visible self-satisfaction is the point: “He preened as everyone praised his speech.”
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Be proud can express healthy satisfaction. Preen usually adds the idea of displaying that satisfaction in a vain or smug way.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: preen in front of + audience; preen oneself on + achievement
common_collocations: preen in front of a crowd

semanticReview.finding: Human self-display sense only; critical connotation and rejected source motive distinguished from actual behaviour.

entry.englishMeaning: to move an event to an earlier time or date

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Time-related phrasal verb: reschedule an event for an earlier date or time.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: the new time may help or inconvenience people depending on the situation.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Polite and practical here: “Could we” asks for a scheduling change and gives the holiday as the reason.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common in British and international workplace English. “Move the review to an earlier date” is clearer across audiences.

when_to_use: Use “bring forward” for this meaning: to move an event to an earlier time or date. For a concrete situation: Could we bring forward the review so that it happens before the holiday?
when_not_to_use: Bring forward means earlier, whereas push back usually means later in scheduling.

advanced_nuance: bring forward: Because date-moving language can be misunderstood across speakers, include the new calendar date explicitly.

memory_practice.memory_sentence: Could we bring forward the appointment to Wednesday?
memory_practice.production_task: Use “bring forward” in your own response: Tell a colleague that a meeting has moved earlier and give both the old and new dates.
memory_practice.recall_question: Without looking at the heading, recall the expression meaning “to move an event to an earlier time or date”. Then explain it in your own words.
memory_practice.recognition_task: Compare these two statements and choose the accurate form or interpretation. A: “We brought the meeting forward from Tuesday to Friday of the same week.” B: “We brought the meeting forward from Friday to Tuesday of the same week.” Explain the difference before checking Mistakes & Differences.

examples.workplace: Could we bring forward the review so that it happens before the holiday?
examples.another_context: Could we bring forward the appointment to Wednesday?

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Could we bring forward the review so that it happens before the holiday?
B: Yes, provided everyone has the material in time to prepare.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: Could we bring forward the review so that it happens before the holiday?
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to move an event to an earlier time or date
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: Pull the event toward today. Here, to move an event to an earlier time or date.

mistakes_differences.correction: We brought the meeting forward from Friday to Tuesday of the same week.
mistakes_differences.common_mistake: We brought the meeting forward from Tuesday to Friday of the same week.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Bring forward means earlier, whereas push back usually means later in scheduling.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: bring forward: bring forward + event + to a date

semanticReview.finding: Bring forward: earlier-date meaning, separated noun form, concrete scheduling examples and date-direction exercise checked; valid non-Overview content retained.

entry.pronunciation: Approximate pronunciation: set UP. Capitals show stress; this is text guidance, not audio.
entry.coreIdea: Create an arrangement so that something can happen.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract phrasal verb for establishing or arranging something; here, create additional choices for a discussion.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: it describes creating options, without guaranteeing they are good ones.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Approving and instructional here: the writer presents making new choices as a skill of effective dialogue.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common across everyday and workplace English. “Create” is a straightforward alternative for choices.

when_to_use: Use set up when creating an arrangement, organization or opportunity.
It can describe organizing a meeting or establishing a group or system.
when_not_to_use: If an arrangement already exists and you only use it, set up would wrongly suggest creating it.
This lesson does not teach the separate sense of tricking someone into trouble.

advanced_nuance: Set up does not guarantee success: a group can be set up and later fail to attract members.
The past form is set up, not setted up. In the source, setting up describes the process of creating additional choices.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture putting the people and arrangements in place for a new activity.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: We set up a group to share practical advice.
memory_practice.recall_question: Does setting up a group mean creating it or necessarily managing it forever?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which has the natural pronoun order? A: She set it up. B: She set up it. Explain your choice.
memory_practice.production_task: Write a message to a colleague offering to set up a fictional meeting. Give its purpose and suggest who should attend.

examples.example_1: We set up a meeting so that both teams could discuss the problem.
examples.example_2: The residents set up a support group for new arrivals.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: We need a chance to compare the two proposals.
B: I'll set up a meeting for tomorrow.
A: Thanks. Please invite both team leaders.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: Search  for the  El usive  And  The  best  at  dialogue  ref use  Sucker's  Choices  by  setting  up  new  choice s.
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: Skilled speakers create new choices instead of accepting only the limited options already offered.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: “I will set up it tomorrow.” A short object pronoun belongs between set and up.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say: “I will set it up tomorrow.” With a noun, “set up the meeting” and “set the meeting up” are both possible.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Set up focuses on creating or arranging something. Run focuses on managing it after it has been established.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: set up + arrangement/group; set + noun + up; set it up

semanticReview.finding: Creation/arrangement sense maintained; separability, irregular past and distinction from ongoing management checked.

entry.englishMeaning: a set of actions intended to restore progress after a problem
entry.coreIdea: A mapped route back after a detour.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract planning phrase: actions designed to get work progressing again after a disruption has occurred.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Constructive: it focuses on restoring progress, while acknowledging that something has gone wrong.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Practical and factual here: new owners and dates explain how the plan responds to the delay.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Neutral professional wording, natural in project updates. Explain the actual recovery actions rather than relying on the phrase alone.

when_to_use: Use “recovery plan” for this meaning: a set of actions intended to restore progress after a problem. For a concrete situation: The recovery plan gives the delayed tasks new owners and dates.
when_not_to_use: A recovery plan focuses on restoring progress after disruption. A contingency plan prepares for a possible disruption; it can include recovery actions.

advanced_nuance: recovery plan: Credibility depends on owners, dates and trade-offs; simply moving the original dates is not a complete recovery plan.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: A mapped route back after a detour.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: The organisers created a recovery plan to reschedule the cancelled sessions.
memory_practice.production_task: Use “recovery plan” in your own response: Outline three actions for recovering a project that is one week late.
memory_practice.recall_question: Without looking at the heading, recall the expression meaning “a set of actions intended to restore progress after a problem”. Then explain it in your own words.
memory_practice.recognition_task: Compare these two statements and choose the accurate form or interpretation. A: “Our recovery plan is designed to avoid further delay.” B: “Our recovery plan is for avoid more delay.” Explain the difference before checking Mistakes & Differences.

examples.workplace: The recovery plan gives the delayed tasks new owners and dates.
examples.another_context: The organisers created a recovery plan to reschedule the cancelled sessions.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: The supplier delay has put us a week behind.
B: Our recovery plan moves two tasks to another team and sets new dates.
A: Who will confirm the revised handover?
B: Mina will check it with both teams today.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: The recovery plan gives the delayed tasks new owners and dates.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: a set of actions intended to restore progress after a problem
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: A mapped route back after a detour. Here, a set of actions intended to restore progress after a problem.

mistakes_differences.correction: Our recovery plan is designed to avoid further delay.
mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Our recovery plan is for avoid more delay.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: A recovery plan focuses on restoring progress after disruption. A contingency plan prepares for a possible disruption; it can include recovery actions.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: recovery plan: a recovery plan for + problem; recovery plan to + verb

semanticReview.finding: Retained useful patterns, examples and practice. Replaced repetitive definition exchange with a concrete delay response and next action; qualified contingency comparison because recovery actions can be planned in advance.

entry.englishMeaning: to depend mainly on one essential fact or factor
entry.coreIdea: Identify the main factor that decides the result.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract phrasal verb for identifying the essential deciding factor; here, the important factor is handling crucial conversations.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: it reduces a complex issue to its central point without automatically judging that point.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Emphatic and summarizing here: “all” gives conversation handling decisive importance.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common in speech and accessible explanatory writing. “Depends mainly on” states the relationship more explicitly.

when_to_use: Use come down to when reducing a complicated decision or situation to its main deciding factor.
It helps summarize what ultimately matters after other details have been considered.
when_not_to_use: Avoid it if several equally important factors must remain separate; naming just one may oversimplify the decision.
This sense does not describe moving physically to a lower place.

advanced_nuance: Come down to expresses the speaker's analysis of what matters most; it is not proof that other factors have no effect.
A question clause uses statement word order: “comes down to how people respond”, not “comes down to how do people respond”.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture several options narrowing to one deciding factor.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: Our choice will come down to cost.
memory_practice.recall_question: What does a speaker emphasize when saying a decision comes down to one factor?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which fits a decision mainly determined by price? A: It comes down to cost. B: Cost is unrelated to it. Explain the relationship.
memory_practice.production_task: Tell a friend how you would choose between two fictional courses. Use come down to and state the main factor.

examples.example_1: The choice of venue comes down to how many guests we expect.
examples.example_2: Both laptops meet my needs, so the decision will come down to price.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Which flat will you choose?
B: It comes down to the journey to work. The smaller one is much closer.
A: Then let's check that bus route.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: It  all  comes  down  to  how  people  handle  crucial  conve rsations.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to depend mainly on one essential fact or factor
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The writer presents people's handling of important conversations as the central factor behind the result.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: “It comes down to choose the right time.” Here to is a preposition, not the start of an infinitive.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say: “It comes down to choosing the right time.” Come down to can also take a noun: “It comes down to timing.”
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Depend on can state any relevant condition. Come down to presents a factor as the central issue after the situation has been simplified.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: subject + come down to + noun/-ing phrase/question clause: it comes down to cost

semanticReview.finding: Central-factor meaning maintained; prepositional to and embedded-clause order checked; oversimplification caveat specific.
